meta.date: ~588 BC (Lehi's death; the psalm written after)

world_behind.title: Blessing over the parents' heads
world_behind.text: To Laman's children Lehi leaves a startling legal transfer: if cursing comes, it will "be answered upon the heads of your parents" (v. 6). Ancient blessing-law let a patriarch redirect liability, and Lehi uses it to fence the grandchildren off from their fathers' account: "the Lord God will not suffer that ye shall perish" (v. 7).

world_behind.title: A death in half a verse
world_behind.text: The man whose sermons filled three chapters gets no deathbed scene: "he waxed old. And it came to pass that he died, and was buried" (v. 12). The record's proportion is deliberate: it spends its metal on what Lehi said, not on grief, and the grief instead breaks out sideways, in the psalm.

world_behind.title: A true Hebrew psalm
world_behind.text: Verses 16–35 run the individual lament's exact form: complaint, remembrance of past mercies, self-exhortation, petition, vow of praise. The family carried Judah's liturgy into exile in someone's memory, and Nephi composes inside the form as one raised on it.

world_behind.title: The soul-track named
world_behind.text: "upon these I write the things of my soul" (v. 15): the two-records doctrine (1 Ne. 9; 19) restated as the psalm's doorway. The history track got the quarrels; these plates get the interior. What follows is the clearest example in the record of what the small plates are for.

spans.text: upon these I write the things of my soul

world_behind.title: The credential list
world_behind.text: Support in the wilderness, preservation on the deep, love "unto the consuming of my flesh" (v. 21), night visions, ministering angels, a body carried to "exceedingly high mountains" (v. 25): the remembrance section is Nephi's inner biography, and it matches the outer one the record has told since the valley of Lemuel.

world_behind.title: Jeremiah in the vow
world_behind.text: "cursed is he that putteth his trust in the arm of flesh" (v. 34) tracks the curse of Lehi's contemporary (Jer. 17:5) nearly clause for clause, including "maketh flesh his arm" (v. 34). The prophet Jerusalem jailed while Lehi fled speaks the psalm's closing doctrine from the brass plates.

words.text: "O wretched man that I am" (v. 17): Paul's exact cry, from the record's least wretched man. The word is the psalm's honest opening position, sorrow "because of my flesh" (v. 17), grief for "mine iniquities" (v. 17), and its placement matters: the confession comes from the obedient son, not the rebels. In this record, closeness to God sharpens self-sight.

words.text: "No longer droop in sin" (v. 28): the psalm's own verb for the state it fights, not collapse but sag, strength leaking rather than breaking. The command is addressed by Nephi to Nephi; drooping in this anatomy is something a soul can be ordered out of, once the remembrance section has done its work.

words.text: "God will give liberally to him that asketh" (v. 35): James's word for how God gives, without stinting and without scolding. The psalm ends by staking everything on that adverb, with one condition kept from the asking side: "my God will give me, if I ask not amiss" (v. 35).

phrases.text: The psalm's verb of appetite: delight "in the scriptures" (v. 15), delight "in the things of the Lord" (v. 16). The phrase becomes Nephi's signature; when he introduces Isaiah's chapters later he will sound it again and again (2 Ne. 11). Delight, in his usage, is not mood but orientation: what the soul keeps returning to.

phrases.term: nevertheless, I know in whom I have trusted
phrases.text: The psalm's hinge, one word wide. Groaning stands on one side, the whole remembrance section on the other, and "nevertheless" (v. 19) carries the turn. Faith in this sentence is not the absence of the groan but the refusal to let the groan finish the sentence.

spans.text: nevertheless

phrases.text: The father's reveille (2 Ne. 1:13), inherited and turned inward. Lehi shouted awake at sleeping sons; Nephi, weeks later, shouts it at himself. The command's change of address is the farewell cycle's quietest lesson: the sermon you receive becomes the one you must preach to your own soul.

The psalmists' bedrock title (Ps. 89:26), planted at the vow of praise and answered at the close by "the rock of my righteousness" (v. 35): the psalm is framed in rock. Between those two fixed points run all the psalm's motions, weeping, waking, petitioning; the ground under them never moves.

phrases.term: shake at the appearance of sin
phrases.text: The petition goes past resisting sin to flinching at its silhouette: "Wilt thou make me that I may shake at the appearance of sin" (v. 31) Asked by the man who just catalogued his own besetting temptations, it is a prayer for recalibrated reflexes, holiness as a startle response, built in by request.

phrases.text: Jeremiah's figure for every human substitute for God, sworn off twice in one verse. The psalm's last doctrine is allegiance: trust placed in God "forever" (v. 34), and the curse quoted over the alternative. The record will keep the phrase as its standing term for misplaced reliance (2 Ne. 28:31).

verses.label: v. 3–7
verses.title: The grandchildren fenced
verses.text: Laman's sons and daughters hear the covenant formula, then the transfer: blessing left so that cursing, if it comes, lands upstream on the parents. Lehi cannot save his firstborn from himself, so he spends his last authority insulating the next generation: "he will be merciful unto you and unto your seed forever" (v. 7).

verses.label: v. 8–11
verses.title: The household, each in turn
verses.text: Lemuel's children get "the same blessing" (v. 9); Ishmael's household is addressed; Sam is folded into Nephi's inheritance, his seed "numbered with his seed" (v. 11). The blessings sort the family into its future: two lines fenced against ruin, one line merged with the promise.

verses.label: v. 12–14
verses.title: A burial, then the old weather
verses.text: Lehi dies between clauses, and "not many days after his death" (v. 13) the anger returns, aimed at Nephi "because of the admonitions of the Lord" (v. 13). The father's absence is measured not in mourning but in how fast the family's storm re-forms without him.

verses.label: v. 15–19
verses.title: Delight and the groan
verses.text: The psalm opens with the soul's appetites, scriptures pondered "for the learning and the profit of my children" (v. 15), then turns without warning: "my heart sorroweth because of my flesh" (v. 17), sins that "so easily beset me" (v. 18), desire to rejoice answered by groaning. Verse 19's nevertheless holds the whole structure while the remembrance loads.

verses.label: v. 20–25
verses.title: The evidence read into the record
verses.text: Support, deliverance on the deep, consuming love, confounded enemies, "he hath heard my cry by day" (v. 23), knowledge by night visions, angels, mountains, things "too great for man" (v. 25). Despair is answered the family way, by inventory; the psalm's faith is documentary before it is emotional.

verses.label: v. 26–30
verses.title: The interrogation, and reveille
verses.text: Three questions turn the evidence on the mood: why droop, why yield, and the most specific: "Why am I angry because of mine enemy" (v. 27) Then the commands: awake, rejoice, do not anger again, do not slacken; and the vow: "I will praise thee forever" (v. 30). Nephi preaches himself out of the pit his honesty dug.

verses.label: v. 31–35
verses.title: The petitions, all as questions
verses.text: Redeem, deliver, make me shake at sin's appearance, shut hell's gates, robe me, straighten the path: every request is a "wilt thou" (v. 31), boldness in the grammar of dependence. The close plants the last stake: no arm of flesh, ask not amiss, and a voice ascending "forever" (v. 35) to "my rock and mine everlasting God" (v. 35).

chapter.title: The record's most human page
chapter.text: Between a funeral and a family rupture, its most obedient man grieves his own sins, names his anger, and talks himself back to praise. The placement is the doctrine: temptation and sorrow cluster at exactly the seams, bereavement, conflict, where readers meet them.

chapter.title: Murmuring and lament are different instruments
chapter.text: The record's great non-murmurer (1 Ne. 18:16) here groans, weeps, and interrogates himself freely. The distinction it draws is directional: murmuring talks about God to men; the psalm talks to God about everything, including the psalmist. Complaint aimed heavenward is worship.

chapter.title: Honesty is the obedient man's burden
chapter.text: Laman never once calls himself wretched; Nephi does. Self-sight in this record scales with light received, which reverses every expectation about who feels their sins: the psalm's grief is a credential, not a contradiction.

chapter.title: Memory defeats mood
chapter.text: The psalm's turn runs on inventory, not willpower: supported, preserved, filled, shown. It is the same instrument Lehi opened the farewell with (rehearsing mercies) and the same one the record itself is: written remembrance as the standing cure for despair.

chapter.title: The besetting sin has a name
chapter.text: Twice the psalm says anger, at enemies with faces (v. 13 supplies them). Its honesty is specific, which is why its comfort is usable: generic wretchedness has no cure, but a named temptation can be renounced, "Do not anger again" (v. 29), and prayed against.

cites.quote: Do not anger again

spans.text: Do not anger again

chapter.title: Petition as interrogative
chapter.text: Every request from verse 31 on is a wilt-thou question: reverent about God's freedom, bold about God's character, and checked by the psalm's own clause, ask not amiss. The record's model prayer is not a demand or a wish but a question asked of someone known.

chapter.title: The farewell cycle ends in a song
chapter.text: Four chapters of blessings close with the father buried and the son singing to the rock. No coronation, no succession scene: the record hands authority forward by showing whose soul still knows where to stand. Chapter 5's rupture is one verse of anger away.

applications.title: Keep a soul-track
applications.text: Alongside whatever calendar or journal you keep, write the things of your soul somewhere distinct: what you pondered, what pierced you, what you would engrave. The psalm exists because Nephi kept two records; your interior deserves its own plates.

applications.title: Let the nevertheless in
applications.text: Next time the groan is honest, groan it, and then practice the psalm's grammar: state the trust before the feelings resolve. "Nevertheless, I know in whom I have trusted" is sayable on bad days; that is what it is for.

applications.title: Run the remembrance section
applications.text: When mood argues that God has gone quiet, answer with inventory: list five specific supports, deliverances, or answers on paper before re-litigating the present. The psalm turns on evidence; yours will too.

applications.title: Name the anger
applications.text: Nephi's besetting sin had a face and a household. Name yours as precisely: the person, the trigger, the recurring hour. "Do not anger again" became possible only after "why am I angry" got an honest answer.

applications.title: Borrow one petition whole
applications.text: Take a single line of the psalm's asking, shut the gates of hell before me, robe me, clear my way, and pray it verbatim for a week over one specific struggle. Borrowed prayers carry you to places your own words have stopped reaching.

applications.title: Audit the arms
applications.text: List what you actually leaned on in the last crisis: savings, charm, a person, competence. Renounce none of the tools, but re-rank them under the rock; the curse in the verse is for trust misfiled, not for means used.

questions.text: If someone read only my "things of the soul," would there be anything to read?
Does closeness to God sharpen or dull my sight of my own sins, and what does that say about the closeness?
What is my sentence after "nevertheless," and can I say it during the groan rather than after?
Which mercies in my own credential list have I never written down anywhere?
What am I angry about right now, and what would the psalm's three questions do to it?
When did I last pray for reflexes, to shake at sin's appearance, rather than only for rescue after it?
